Everything this project has built, measured and learned — including the result that changed what the paper is about. Written so someone joining today can be useful by this afternoon.

6-stage pipeline 5 hospitals 33 B VLM baseline 122 tests passing Paper drafted
01 — Start here

What this project is

One paragraph, then the detail.

A panoramic dental X-ray — an OPG — is the wide photograph a dentist takes that shows every tooth in one image. We built software that looks at one and produces a report: which tooth is which, and which teeth have problems. Two problems specifically: cavities (caries) and gum-and-bone disease (periodontal bone loss).

In plain words

Imagine a photo of all 32 teeth in someone's mouth. Our program draws a box around each tooth, gives each one its proper dental number, and then says "this one has a hole in it." That's it. Everything below is about how well it actually does that — and one surprising discovery about how we were measuring it.

The six stages

The system is a chain. Each stage hands its output to the next, which means a mistake early on cannot be repaired later — a fact that turns out to matter a great deal.

1

Find the teeth

A detector (YOLOv11l-seg) draws a box around every tooth it can see.

2

Name the teeth

Each box gets an FDI number — the international code dentists use, like "16" for the upper-right first molar. One number per tooth, assigned so no two teeth claim the same code.

3

Look for cavities

A small classifier decides, tooth by tooth, whether there is decay.

4

Look for bone loss

A second classifier checks for gum disease. This branch does not survive being moved to a new hospital — we report that as a finding, not a feature.

5

Join it up

All findings are matched to their tooth number.

6

Write the report

Out comes a structured record and a picture with the findings drawn on.

The whole thing is 83.6 million parameters and runs in 2.39 seconds per image on an ordinary CPU — no graphics card needed. Keep that number; it comes back.

Five hospitals, four datasets

Why "leak-free" and "locked" matter

If a program is tested on a picture it already studied, it looks clever without being clever. So 86 DENTEX images were thrown out of testing because the system had seen them in training, leaving 164. And the Ningxia hospitals are treated as sealed: we never train on them, never tune to them, and record every single time we look. That discipline is the most valuable thing this project has.

03 — The main finding

A program that never looks at the X-ray scores as well as ours

This is the result the paper is now built around. It is uncomfortable, it is real, and it is more interesting than the number it replaced.

We wanted to know what our cavity score actually meant. So we lined up four systems against the same 164 images with the same scorer, each one given less information than the last: our pipeline, a very large AI model, a smaller one, and finally a program that is never shown the X-ray at all — it just says "the eight molars have cavities" every single time.

The program that never sees the image scored highest.
Why that happens — the 10-year-old version

Cavities are not spread evenly around the mouth. They pile up in the big back teeth, the molars. So if you simply always say "the back teeth are bad," you will be right a lot of the time — not because you looked, but because that is where cavities live. Our program had to beat that lucky guess to prove it was really looking. On this test, it didn't.

On the second, location-based measurement the constant led by 4.59 percentage points, 95% CI [+0.60, +8.89] — and it did not win by carpet-bombing: it flagged only 14% more teeth, at the same hit rate.

Then the external hospitals disagreed

We expected the four Ningxia hospitals to confirm it. They didn't. Pooled, the difference is −0.89 points, CI [−4.88, +3.01] — statistically indistinguishable. Per hospital it swings from +15.8 at one site to −10.6 at another.

So the honest claim across all five hospitals is not "the constant is better." It is that the two are not reliably distinguishable — which is still a serious statement about the measurement, and it is what the paper says.

04 — The AI-model comparison

We tested a 33-billion-parameter model. It answered confidently to a blank image.

The vision–language model arm, run on rented H100 hardware, and the control that makes its score interpretable.

A vision–language model (VLM) is the kind of AI you can show a picture to and ask a question in plain English. We tested two sizes of Qwen2.5-VL — 7B and 32B (33.45 billion parameters as actually loaded, using 70 GB of GPU memory). Both were given every advantage: the numbering system explained in the prompt, told teeth may be missing, and their answers parsed forgivingly. Our pipeline got no such help.

33.45 B
Parameters in the large model
70.1 GB
GPU memory it needed
83.6 M
Our whole pipeline, on a CPU
≈550×
Size difference — and it still loses

Three things we learned

Bigger helped. 7B scored 0.149; 32B scored 0.246. Scale is not nothing.

Better prompting made it worse. Giving it worked examples — 2-shot, then 4-shot — dropped it to 0.066 then 0.034. The reason is specific and worth knowing: the examples taught it to stay silent. Empty answers went from 56 of 164 images to 123 of 164. One score in the table even improves as this happens, because 16 images genuinely have no cavities and an empty answer is right on those. Reported alone that column would be true and completely misleading.

It answered a picture with no teeth in it. We showed both models a blank grey rectangle and a square of random static. The smaller model returned the same confident list of tooth numbers it gives a real X-ray.

Why this control matters

If a model gives the same answer to a real X-ray and to a grey rectangle, then its score is not measuring whether it can see teeth. It's measuring what it guesses when it has nothing to go on. Without running that test, 0.246 looks like "pretty good". With it, you know what the number is made of.

Being precise: the larger model correctly answered "NONE" to the blank image. It was the random-static image that it answered with a full list of molars. That distinction is in the paper — an earlier draft overstated it and was corrected.

05 — What the system genuinely does well

Three things a lucky guess cannot do

The constant can win a set-membership score. It cannot name a tooth, know when it is unsure, or behave sensibly in a new hospital.

It names teeth correctly

End-to-end, the system gets the right tooth number 58.3% of the time (CI [53.9, 62.8]). That sounds mediocre until you see where the loss happens: 29.4% of teeth are never detected at all, and no naming model can recover a tooth that was never found. Of the teeth the detector does find, naming is correct 82.6% of the time (CI [79.1, 85.8]). Both numbers must be reported — either alone misleads.

And the mistakes are mostly gentle: of 115 wrong codes, 89 (77.4%) are off-by-one — the right region, the neighbouring tooth. Only 2.4% of found teeth land in the wrong quadrant of the mouth.

It knows when it is unsure — and that is measurable

If the system declines the quarter of cases it is least confident about, accuracy rises: tooth naming 0.826 → 0.885, cavity detection 0.797 → 0.940.

But a rise like that can happen for a boring reason — throw away hard cases and what's left looks easy. So we ran the control: shuffle the confidence scores, breaking the link between "sure" and "correct" while keeping everything else identical. The gains collapse to +0.03 and +0.00. The improvement is real and it lives in the ranking.

Its confidence scores mean something — after a repair

Out of the box, when the cavity model said "90% sure", it was right far less than 90% of the time. Expected calibration error: 0.136. The standard fix (temperature scaling) made it worse — which told us the problem was structural, not a simple scale. Isotonic regression fixed it to 0.043, a 68% improvement.

06 — The failure we publish

Bone loss works beautifully, then stops working

Reported as a measured negative result, not hidden in an appendix.

On the data it was trained on, the bone-loss branch scores 0.923 macro-F1. Move it to another dataset and it essentially stops firing: 0.7% of DENTEX teeth, 1.4–5.6% across the four external hospitals.

We tested the obvious explanation — that the detector upstream was to blame — by swapping the detector. That swap improved tooth naming by +12.0 points and cavity agreement by +7.7. It moved bone loss by nothing. So the shared-cause theory is dead, and we say so.

Why we report this instead of quietly dropping it

A screening tool that fails silently is more dangerous than one that fails visibly. And a paper arguing that people should publish their baselines has no standing to hide its own bad result.

07 — Publishability

Is this publishable? Yes — as an evaluation paper

An honest read of where this stands against a real venue.

Judged as "we built a cavity detector," the numbers are unremarkable and a reviewer will find the constant baseline in ten minutes. Judged as "here is why tooth-level cavity scores cannot be interpreted without a floor," this is a genuine, novel, well-controlled contribution — and the evidence is unusually strong.

What makes it publishable

  • Three system classes, two unrelated metrics, five hospitals — the finding is not one lucky measurement.
  • External testing on four outside hospitals. In our own review of 49 task-relevant papers, only two do this at all.
  • Every comparison carries a confidence interval, clustered over images rather than teeth — because teeth from one mouth are not independent observations.
  • Every claim has a control. Shuffled confidences for abstention, blank and noise images for the VLMs, held-out fitting for the constant.
  • Negative results are reported, including two that are unfavourable to us.
  • Pre-registered thresholds that were not moved when the numbers arrived — including one bar we missed and reported as missed.

What still holds it back

  • No clinician comparison. The single largest gap. We do not know how any of these systems compare to a dentist on these images.
  • Reference count is 26; a journal will want 35–50.
  • Four compliance items are unresolved, and two are live protocol breaches rather than paperwork.
  • The bone-loss result is not reproducible on this machine and is reported as secondary because of it.
The honest verdict

Today, this is a solid mid-tier conference paper. With a reader study — even two dentists over 100 images — it becomes a credible journal submission, because external testing across four hospitals plus a clinician reference is a combination this literature rarely has. That single experiment is the highest-value thing left to do.

08 — The manuscript

Where the paper stands

8 pages, IEEE format, 5 figures, 26 verified references. Author fields are deliberately blank pending the team's decision.

paper/main.tex · paper/main.pdf · paper/paper.txt · paper/source.bib

What was checked, and what it found

The manuscript went through a verification pass that found real errors — worth knowing about, because the same failure modes will recur:

  • 7 citation errors. Two invented titles, one wrong publication year, and a claim about gum disease attributed to two papers about entirely different conditions. All compiled silently.
  • 4 wrong DOIs out of ten added entries, corrected against publisher records. Four more were left deliberately blank rather than guessed.
  • A figure built from the wrong detector — the superseded one, not the pipeline default.
  • A claim we never actually counted ("no paper reports a baseline"), now flagged for softening. It is the most exposed sentence in the paper, because the contribution depends on that gap being real.

Re-run any time: scripts/audit_citations.py · scripts/check_text_reuse.py

09 — What is left

Submission to-do, cross-checked against the repository

Every item below was verified against the actual code and results before being marked. Several arrived on the list already done.

DONE PARTIAL OPEN BLOCKED

Technical & scientific

Reproduce the periodontal experiment BLOCKED

773 of 1,558 validation crops carry ±15% jitter applied with offsets that were never saved — irreproducible by construction. The original un-rotated radiographs are also absent from this machine. The fallback is already taken: the result appears as a measured negative, never as a headline. Seeds, checkpoints and hashes are now saved going forward.

95% confidence intervals MOSTLY DONE

Already present for detection recall, end-to-end naming, naming-of-detected, internal lesion agreement, all four external sites, the pooled result, paired detector deltas, both abstention gains, both constant-vs-pipeline comparisons, and the third-corpus ablation. Still missing: detection mAP and per-class precision/recall — both need per-item prediction dumps, which is cheap CPU work.

Uncertainty on external testing DONE

Per site, pooled, and around the difference. The 26-point per-site spread is reported as a finding rather than smoothed away.

Distinguish the metrics DONE

DENTEX uses IoU ≥ 0.30 with centroid fallback; external cohorts use centroid containment. Documented with the reason: external lesions are 89–3,090 px blobs inside ~25,000 px tooth boxes, so IoU would score ~0% by construction, regardless of model quality.

Title DECISION — current is "What a Tooth-Level Score Cannot Tell You…"; the proposed alternative is more literal and more searchable. Team call.

One primary research question PARTIAL — implied throughout, never stated in one sentence.

2–4 explicit hypotheses OPEN

Abstract structure CONFLICT — DECIDE

The current abstract deliberately withholds the result to make the reader open the paper — an explicit earlier instruction. This to-do asks for Background → Problem → Methods → Results → Conclusion, which requires giving the result away in sentence four. Both are defensible; they are mutually exclusive. Recommendation: structured, if the target is a medical journal. Flagging rather than silently choosing.

The four blockers that are not engineering

None of these can be fixed with code, and two are live protocol breaches:

  1. IRB not started. Longest lead time of anything open. Gates the ethics statement and the reader study.
  2. A Tufts Drive folder is browsable without sign-in — the licence forbids redistribution.
  3. DENTEX and Ningxia licences never read or recorded.
  4. SDH metadata/index.csv sits beside images/, voiding that copy's de-identification.

The one house rule worth knowing on day one

Undocumented results are lost results. If you train something, measure something, or fix something, it goes in RESULTS_LOG.md before you stop — and if a number cannot be traced to a saved output, it gets marked unverified. This project once spent three months with a README claiming finished models were still in progress.

Compiled 28 August 2026 from the repository's own records. Every figure is generated from saved evaluation artefacts rather than transcribed, and every number here traces to RESULTS_LOG.md, model_metrics.md or a JSON under outputs/.
